Divide the United States and Israel from the Arab states
Iraq-based Axis of Resistance actors have very likely launched at least four drones targeting Saudi Arabia within the past 20 days.[27] Saudi security sources told US-funded regional media on October 22 that the drones targeted unspecified “vital sites.”[28] Saudi Arabia has reportedly informed the Iraqi federal government of the attacks.[29] The report did not specify where in Iraq the launches originated, but Iraqi authorities have reportedly increased surveillance over militia sites in Maysan Province over the past two weeks that they suspect Iranian-backed Iraqi militias are using to conduct attacks.[30] IRGC-managed Iraqi militia cells based along the Iraq-Iran border, including in Maysan Province, have conducted multiple attacks on neighboring countries in recent months, including a September 10 attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline.[31] The Houthis, who maintain an active presence in Iraq, reportedly coordinated some of these cross-border attacks with Iraqi militias.[32] It is possible that Iraqi fighters, Houthi fighters, or a combination of Iraqi and Houthi forces launched the drones at Saudi Arabia. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and other regional countries from Iraq by any Iranian partner or proxy support Iranian objectives to compel the United States to end the war in terms favorable to Iran by imposing increasing costs on US partners and allies in the region, including by imposing economic costs through attacks on energy infrastructure.
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to advance into contested territory south of Taiz City, likely to try to break the Houthis’ encirclement of government-aligned forces in central Taiz Governorate. Yemeni government-aligned forces advanced to Jabal Manara in al Misrakh District on October 22, which the Houthis previously occupied, according to Yemeni and DC-based Yemen analyst sources.[33] Yemeni government-aligned forces have advanced into al Misrakh District and engaged Houthi fighters in the area in recent days, likely in order to try to break the Houthis' encirclement of central Taiz Governorate. The Houthis fully encircled the city on October 12.[34]
Yemeni government-aligned forces’ advances into al Misrakh District come amid the continued success of Yemeni government-aligned forces’ efforts to repel Houthi advances into the “Old Airport” neighborhood on the western outskirts of Taiz City on October 22.[35] Yemeni government-aligned forces similarly repelled Houthi attempts to advance into the area on October 17 and 18.[36] The “Old Airport” neighborhood sits along a major road leading into Taiz City that the Houthis have sought to capture in recent weeks.[37]
The Houthis have continued to attack targets across Saudi Arabia to impose economic and political costs on Saudi Arabia and compel Saudi Arabia to capitulate to Houthi demands. The Saudi Joint Forces Command reported that Saudi air defenses intercepted one ballistic missile over Najran, southern Saudi Arabia, on October 22.[38] Saudi air defenses also intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and Khamis Mushait and two drones over Saudi Arabia’s southern region on October 23.[39] The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil facilities, airports, and other civilian infrastructure as part of their ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[40]

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Former adviser to the Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia's occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”. Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to "Novorossiya" — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people. Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine . Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv's surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.
Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB). The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.5 to 13.5 percent in 2027 — only 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points below the current rate. The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.8 percent. The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.1 and 7.6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics. Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.5 and one percent. Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.
The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase export revenues, despite ongoing fiscal inflationary pressures.[18] The Central Bank’s apparent success in avoiding further interest rate reductions at this time indicates that Putin has likely become more tolerant of contractionary monetary policy. Putin has recently prioritized reducing inflation to secure support amongst the Russian population by attempting to reduce the economic effects of Russian war spending, a prioritization that may have led him to accept Nabiullina’s fiscal policy for now.[19] Keeping the key rate at the current level will likely suppress wage growth and limit the amount of capital available to the Russian DIB, which may prevent Putin from achieving his goals of raising Russians’ effective purchasing power and maintaining the DIB’s production capacity. It remains difficult to assess, however, what effect fiscal policy will have on wage inflation and Russians’ quality of life, since Russia’s persistent labor shortages drive wage inflation for employed individuals while households face pressures that nominal wage figures do not capture.[20]
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23. Romanian President Nicusor Dan stated on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck a Comoros-flagged Khoryv cargo ship “near Romanian territorial waters” and added that the strike is a consequence of “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”[21] The Romanian Naval Authority reported that the Khoryv vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (around 24 kilometers and just outside of the Romanian territorial waters) off the coast of Constanta, Romania.[22] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the October 23 drone strike yet another “Russian escalation” in the Black Sea.[23] Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the country's shoreline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.[24] The October 23 drone strike comes against the backdrop of recent escalating Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including likely Russian drone strikes against two commercial tankers within Romanian territorial waters on October 14 and 15 and strikes against civilian vessels in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) overnight on October 12 to 13.[25] The Moldovan police separately reported on October 23 that drone debris fell up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica, Telenesti Raion, Moldova.[26] These continuous, likely Russian violations of Moldovan and Romanian sovereign territory demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to pursue strike tactics that may directly impact the territory of NATO or NATO-aligned states.[27]
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23. Ukrainian and Russian authorities reported on October 23 that Ukraine and Russia exchanged 270 prisoners each.[28] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Russia returned nine civilian prisoners back to Ukraine as part of the exchange.[29] Ukrainian Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of POWs reported that the October 23 POW exchange is the third stage of a combined prisoner swap that began on August 19, 2026.[30] Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets separately reported that Russia and Ukraine exchanged seven more civilians on October 23.[31]

We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian forces launched a large strike package toward Moscow City, prompting the suspension of operations at all four Moscow area airports and the evacuation of government administrative buildings. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on October 23 that 155 Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow Oblast overnight on October 22 and 23.[32] Russian state aviation regulator Rosaviatsia announced on October 23 that Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports — all four major airports servicing Moscow City — introduced temporary restrictions.[33] A Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel posted an image on October 23 showing drone debris on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo Airport.[34] The channel also published footage on October 23 purporting to show balloons flying over Moscow City, purportedly carrying explosives or small drones.[35] Russian opposition outlet Astra reported on October 23 that Russian authorities evacuated the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which reportedly houses offices for the Russian Ministries of Economic Development, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Ministry of Digital Development, and the Federal Agency for Technical Regulation and Metrology.[36]
Ukrainian forces conducted a series of long-range strikes against a Russian defense industrial facility, a chemical production plant, and administrative and military infrastructure in Russia. Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows the moment of a likely Ukrainian missile strike against the Proton plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 161 kilometers from the frontline).[37] A Ukrainian OSINT channel stated that reportedly Ukrainian Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the plant.[38] Ukrainian defense source Militarnyi reported that the plant manufactures components for the Russian S-71 Kover cruise missiles, Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.[39] Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows a Ukrainian FP-1 drone approaching the Azot UralKhim Chemical Plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai (roughly 1,585 kilometers from the international border) and smoke plumes rising from the facility.[40] Perm Krai governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian forces struck and damaged an industrial facility.[41] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted footage on October 23 purporting to show Ukrainian forces striking a Russian Federal Taxation Service data center in Gorodets, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast (roughly 785 kilometers from the international border).[42] Nizhny Novgorod Oblast Governor Gleb Nikitin acknowledged on October 23 that drone debris damaged unspecified infrastructure in Gorodets raion.[43] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted on October 23 an image showing smoke plumes near Baltimore Air Base in Voronezh City (roughly 190 kilometers from the international border).[44] The channel reported that preliminary information indicates that Ukrainian forces targeted the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University and an adjacent military aircraft parking area.[45] Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian drones targeted Voronezh City.[46]
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in northern Sumy Oblast on October 23 but did not advance.[47]
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach Kharkiv City
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions northeast and northwest of Kharkiv City. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions southeast of Khrypuny (northeast of Kharkiv City) and south of Nova Kozacha (northwest of Kharkiv City), according to geolocated footage published on October 20 and 22, respectively, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations northeast of Velykyi Burluk on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[49]
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblas t
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kupyansk direction on October 22 and 23 but did not make confirmed advances.[50]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Borova direction on October 23.
Russian Main Effort: Capture Ukraine's Fortress Belt and complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the northwest
Russian objective: Seize Lyman and cross the Siverskyi Donets River to support a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt – assessed objective of the Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Lyman direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[51] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces are developing an offensive from Yampil (southeast of Lyman) towards Ozerne (southwest of Yampil) and Dibrova (west of Yampil).[52]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the east
Russian objective: Advance on Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka from the east – assessed objective of the Russian 3rd Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations east of Slovyansk on October 23.[53] Donetsk Oblast Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin ordered on October 22 the mandatory evacuation of all families with children in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk hromadas due to ongoing Russian strikes against civilian and residential infrastructure.[54]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the south
Russian objective: Advance on Kostyantynivka and Druzhkivka from the south and southwest, east of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 8th Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka. Ukrainian forces recently advanced in northern Sofiivka, according to geolocated footage published on October 22.[55]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #4 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the southwest
Russian objective: Conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt from near Dobropillya and Pokrovsk west of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 51st Combined Arms Army and Central Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces recently conducted an infiltration mission in southern Dobropillya. Russian forces are operating in southern Dobropillya, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses was a Russian infiltration mission.[56] Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets reported on October 21 that Russian forces infiltrated southern Dobropillya.[57]
Russian sources continue to use likely AI-generated or AI-altered footage to make aggrandized claims in the Dobropillya direction. A Russian source published footage on October 23 purportedly showing Russian forces raising flags in Vesele Pole (north of Dobropillya and roughly 12 kilometers from the furthest assessed extent of Russian advances).[58] ISW has reason to believe that the Russian flag raising video may be AI-generated or AI-altered, which would be consistent with previous Russian information operations that use AI footage to claim battlefield advances.[59]
Russian Supporting Effort: Advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian objective: Interdict Ukrainian ground lines of communication that support Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast and envelop Ukrainian positions in southwestern Donetsk Oblast – assessed objective of elements of the Russian Central and Eastern groupings of forces
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Novopavlivka and Oleksandrivka directions on October 23.
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City – assessed objective of the Russian Eastern and Dnepr Grouping of Forces
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Hulyaipole direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked in the area.[60]
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions west of Orikhiv. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions in eastern Stepnohirsk, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[61] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces advanced south of Lukyanivske (west of Orikhiv).[62]
Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian drone operators in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies manpower concentration near Kamyanka, Zaporizhia Oblast (roughly 31 kilometers from the frontline) on October 22 or overnight on October 22 to 23.[63]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Kherson direction on October 23.

items.title: Energy Transfer vs. Kinder Morgan: Which Natural Gas Pipeline Stock Is the Better Buy for the AI Power Boom? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Energy Transfer vs. Kinder Morgan: Which Natural Gas Pipeline Stock Is the Better Buy for the AI Power Boom?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Energy Transfer ( ET +2.05% ) and Kinder Morgan ( KMI +2.11% ) are two of the largest midstream businesses in North America. Although both have cut their dividends in the past, they are growing them at a steady clip today. However, as artificial intelligence (AI) shifts the demand story in the electricity sector, Kinder Morgan is likely the better-positioned business, if you're willing to pay for it. Here's what you need to know to choose between these two midstream operators.
There is a massive effort underway to build the infrastructure that supports artificial intelligence . However, at its core, AI is just a fancy computer program. It doesn't exist without electricity. The more AI infrastructure that's built, the more electricity is needed. Between 2024 and 2030, the International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from AI to increase "more than four times faster than the growth of total electricity consumption from all other sectors."
The world needs more electricity in a big way, with some estimates that electricity demand will grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045. That's up from growth of just 10% between 2005 and 2025. Pipeline companies are a vital part of supplying this electricity because natural gas is increasingly being used to generate power.
There's more good news. Businesses like Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan largely charge fees for the use of their energy infrastructure assets. So while commodity prices can be highly volatile, midstream companies largely sidestep that risk. The volume flowing through their systems is more important than the price of what is being moved. In other words, Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan are likely to benefit from AI regardless of what happens to natural gas prices.

Which is better positioned: Energy Transfer or Kinder Morgan?
There is a notable difference between Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan regarding natural gas. Natural gas makes up around 35% of Energy Transfer's business, while Kinder Morgan's exposure is 67%. In fact, Kinder Morgan claims to own the largest natural gas transmission network in the United States.
From this perspective, Kinder Morgan is better positioned to benefit from increasing demand for the natural gas used to generate electricity. If that is all you are focused on, it is probably the better choice for your portfolio.

The problem is that Kinder Morgan's dividend yield is only 3.4%, which is far below the 6.7% yield that you could collect from Energy Transfer. To buy either for a dividend portfolio , you need to accept that both have both cut their dividends in the past. They are growing again, as noted above. In fact, slow and steady dividend growth is likely to be the norm for each at this point. Still, if income is your real focus, then Energy Transfer is the obvious winner. And, while it may not benefit as much as Kinder Morgan from AI's voracious appetite for electricity, it will still benefit.
The simple answer here is that Kinder Morgan is more leveraged to natural gas than Energy Transfer. But that's looking at the comparison in something of a vacuum. Wall Street clearly knows Kinder Morgan is tied into the AI story, and it has been priced accordingly. That has left the stock with a relatively low yield in a sector known for providing attractive yields. In other words, if you are trying to live off of the income your portfolio generates, you may be better off with less natural gas exposure and more yield. And that could make Energy Transfer the more appropriate choice.

items.title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing
items.summary: Police have launched a manhunt for the building's owner and contractor after the multi-storey building collapsed while still under construction.
items.content:
Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, on Friday, as a search continues for five still missing.
Police said on Saturday that a manhunt had been launched for the building's owner and the contractor responsible for the site.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.
Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.
The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.
Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.
On Friday, Murkomen said that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble.
The two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital, police said.
Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.
Image caption, Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.
Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable.
In a statement it warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would "face the full force of the law".
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

items.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
items.summary: Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop retreat
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
Image caption, The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website , external .
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

items.title: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Amazon ( AMZN -0.95% ) recently launched a new software tool that will allow its custom Trainium AI chips to run code written in the most popular AI coding language without modification. It's a move aimed at boosting the potential for Amazon's custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) to take market share away from Nvidia 's ( NVDA -0.59% ) widely used graphics processing units as demand for AI chips continues to swell.
Amazon isn't the only tech giant working on its own AI chips for commercial use. Alphabet  recently began making its custom AI chips available for sale directly to enterprises, rather than limiting them to being leased through Google Cloud. However, investors shouldn't expect these developments to have a meaningful effect on Nvidia's financial results.
Amazon's AI chip business wrapped up the second quarter with a $25 billion annual revenue run rate. That's not small, but it pales in comparison to the $96.2 billion in revenue Nvidia booked in its fiscal 2027 second quarter alone, or the more than $300 billion it booked over the past four quarters.

While Amazon's push to commercialize its custom chips could boost sales, the largest tech companies are still rushing to buy Nvidia chips. That's how Nvidia managed to produce 106% year-over-year revenue growth in its most recent quarter, and CEO Jensen Huang says that AI demand is still accelerating.
If anything, Amazon's AI chips can become niche hardware in the industry. Since the AI build-out has been so expansive, it may provide enough room for high, sustained revenue growth rates. If Amazon's chip business can generate net profit margins similar to Nvidia's, that should be enough to boost Amazon's stock price.
Another point supporting the view that Amazon's AI chips won't significantly impact Nvidia's business is that Amazon is still buying Nvidia chips. In fact, it has built up a stockpile of billions of dollars' worth of them that it doesn't yet have the data center infrastructure and connected electricity supply to power up.
Nvidia's processors have become the most reliable option for providing high-end compute in an industry that values speed and will pay a premium for flawless execution. Even as Amazon touts the value of its own chips for the narrower workloads they are designed to handle, for flexible compute power, the tech leader still turns to Nvidia.
Notably, those stockpiled supplies of chips and data center servers highlight that electrical supplies will remain a major bottleneck for AI infrastructure expansion. Still, hyperscalers aren't waiting for that problem to be resolved completely, and continue to accelerate their capital expenditures.
Nvidia's guidance implies that its business is still growing at a substantial rate despite the intensifying competition. Its fiscal 2027 third-quarter guidance calls for $108 billion in revenue at the midpoint, which would amount to 12.3% sequential growth. That guidance supports Huang's claim that AI demand is accelerating.
While more rivals are likely to enter the expanding AI chip market, Nvidia remains the clear leader in data center chips.

Philips helped Taiwan begin its decades-long technology transformation
Li Kwoh-ting pursued foreign expertise to build Taiwan's domestic electronics industry
TSMC manufactures advanced chips, while ASML builds equipment used in production
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has recently discussed how Taiwan's semiconductor leadership emerged through decades of industrial partnerships, government planning and manufacturing expertise.
During a recent conversation with Lex Fridman, Huang discussed how European technology relationships helped establish capabilities that later supported Taiwan's electronics industry.
The island now manufactures more than 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors, giving its relatively small territory enormous importance to global technology supply chains.
Philips helped establish Taiwan's electronics foundations
The story dates back to the 1950s, when Taiwanese economic planner Li Kwoh-ting pursued foreign partnerships to develop domestic manufacturing technology.
His efforts included attracting Dutch electronics manufacturer Philips, whose involvement helped introduce industrial knowledge and production capabilities into Taiwan's developing electronics sector.
Philips subsequently became part of the historical background behind companies that helped shape semiconductor manufacturing and equipment development.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) eventually became central to advanced chip production, while Dutch equipment supplier ASML emerged as a leading manufacturer of lithography systems.

These businesses occupy different positions within semiconductor supply chains, with TSMC fabricating integrated circuits and ASML supplying machinery used during chip production.
Their historical connections to Philips help explain how international industrial relationships contributed to Taiwan's technological development.
However, their subsequent success involved different corporate histories, investments and technological advances rather than one partnership determining the industry's eventual direction.
Taiwan's manufacturing capabilities developed through sustained industrial expansion, foreign relationships and growing demand for increasingly sophisticated electronic components.
Computer manufacturing created another opportunity for Taiwan
Taiwan's electronics industry continued expanding as international demand for personal computers created new opportunities for component suppliers.
IBM helped accelerate this development when it published specifications for its personal computer architecture, enabling other manufacturers to build compatible machines and supporting components.
Taiwanese businesses capitalised on the growing market by designing chipsets and supplying computer components to manufacturers.
TSMC and United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) subsequently became important semiconductor manufacturers, although their expansion involved distinct strategies and developments across the industry.
The growth of compatible personal computers also created opportunities for motherboard suppliers serving companies assembling and selling complete systems.
Michael Dell , who founded his computer business during this period, initially built machines using commercially available components, including parts sourced through international supply chains.
Taiwanese suppliers formed part of that developing network, although Dell's eventual success also depended on his direct sales approach and business operations.
IBM's influence therefore represents a separate stage in Taiwan's industrial development, rather than a direct consequence of Philips' earlier involvement.
Huang's account connects foreign investment, manufacturing expertise and changing market opportunities to explain Taiwan's rise within the semiconductor industry.
Its current leadership, however, rests on decades of further investment, engineering advances and specialised production capabilities.
The island's concentration of advanced chip manufacturing has become particularly significant as AI increases demand for sophisticated processors .
Governments and technology companies are consequently seeking reliable supplies, while Taiwan's manufacturing expertise remains difficult to reproduce quickly elsewhere.

Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in
The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike .
"The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation."
The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks.
Chair of the Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the William McChesney Martin Jr. Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, July 29, 2026.
Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016.
After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year.
Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up.
Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank.
What interest rate hikes mean for you and the economy
"Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements.
"This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added.
The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank.
A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again.
Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring.
Oil prices surge after Trump vows retaliation for Iranian attack
Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses.
Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%.

"I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in."
Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year.
The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said.
"We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added.
Fed holds interest rates steady as economy weathers resurgent inflation
Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions.
In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision.
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage, which closely tracks the 10-year Treasury yield, stands at 6.66%, its highest level in a year, Freddie Mac data on Thursday showed.
"That market-delivered tightening is why the Fed could hold," Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of data firm GLJ Research, told ABC News in a statement. "The market did the work; Warsh banked it."
A wide gap between the benchmark rate set by central bankers, the federal funds rate, and the market for Treasuries could pose challenges for policymakers, however. Investors may seek to exploit the gap, and economic tumult could result, Gerald Epstein, a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told ABC News.
"Eventually, the Fed would need to raise interest rates," Epstein said.
Too much focus on wonky economic questions risks overlooking the political dynamic surrounding interest rate policy, some economists said.
President Donald Trump pressured Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, in an effort to reduce interest rates. The Department of Justice opened an unprecedented criminal probe into Powell, which he viewed as part and parcel of the pressure campaign. Trump has denied any involvement in the probe, which the DOJ later dropped .
Warsh has voiced support for the independence of the Fed, but he may seek to avoid rate increases even as he vows to fight inflation, especially as the political calendar barrels toward the November midterm elections, Epstein said.
"The elephant in the room is that the hawkish tone of the Fed chair is at odds with the preference of the White House for a rate cut," Brusuelas said.

items.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
items.summary: Officials have so far managed to avoid a repeat of last weekend's rioting and looting as hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishes
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.
After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.
Image caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.
Image caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in Bordeaux
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
NuÃ±ez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.
Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Image caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

items.content:
Dems, voting-rights groups challenge bid to block Alaska certification
Democratic groups and voting-rights advocates are seeking to join a federal lawsuit to stop the Justice Department's effort to prevent Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The requests come from Alaskans for Mary, the campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, the Democratic Party's Senate campaign committee, and a separate group including the League of Women Voters of Alaska, Common Cause, and two individual voters.
Together, the groups argue that the federal executive branch lacks legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration with early voting already underway.
Alaska Senate Candidates: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) (L), and Rep. Mary Peltola (D-AK).
Democratic groups and voting-rights advocates are seeking to join a federal lawsuit to stop the Justice Department's effort to prevent Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The requests come from Alaskans for Mary, the campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, the Democratic Party's Senate campaign committee, and a separate group including the League of Women Voters of Alaska, Common Cause and two individual voters.
Together, the groups argue that the executive branch lacks legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration with early voting already underway.
In court filings submitted Friday, the groups contend that the litigation — which President Donald Trump confirmed he personally ordered — seeks an extraordinary remedy: an investigation into whether voters who selected another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent senator.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file the lawsuit: "I'm the one that said 'do it.'"
The move drew swift bipartisan backlash, including from Alaska's Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who said on social media , "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
The legal battle centers on Daniel J. Sullivan, a non-incumbent challenger sharing a near-identical name with incumbent GOP Senator Daniel S. Sullivan. Alaska election officials initially removed the challenger from the ballot after a complaint from the state Republican Party, but state courts ordered his inclusion on the ballot.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that decision and directed election officials to clearly distinguish the two men.
The ballot now lists Sen. Sullivan as the "incumbent" and Republican, while the other Sullivan has no party registration.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 22, seeking an order to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election if the incumbent loses.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Justice Department on August 12, 2026 in Washington, DC.
The proposed intervenors say the department's approach would force Alaska voters to choose between electing the president's preferred candidate and risking the state being barred from certifying its election results.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argue that the lawsuit directly threatens their interests because it could prevent Peltola from taking office even if she wins the election under Alaska's ranked-choice system.
They also question whether Alaska state officials will mount a sufficiently vigorous defense, given that the state's Division of Elections previously tried to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot before a state court overturned the move.
The DSCC and Alaskans for Mary are asking the court to grant them defendant-intervenor status so they can formally file motions to dismiss the lawsuit.
The Democrats argue that while the DOJ has cited the National Voter Registration Act as the legal basis for its lawsuit, the statute contains no provision authorizing the federal government to dictate candidate eligibility or ballot layout, which are state matters under the Constitution.
Legal experts have echoed those concerns, noting that relying on the NVRA's general preamble language to halt state election certification lacks precedent.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska  and  Common Cause  filed separately, warning that the DOJ's demand to investigate voter intent presents severe constitutional hazards.
The filings note that the DOJ has offered no mechanism to determine whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan intended to vote for the incumbent.
Blocking certification, the groups argue, would disenfranchise Alaskans by denying them representation and injecting chaos into the election outcome.
Both organizations are asking the court for permission to join the case as defendants. The Democratic groups say they intend to seek dismissal if the court grants their motion.

Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.
Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times .
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics .
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.
Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year , almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”
Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic
Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.
Other restaurants have opened in Dubai , including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.
Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.
Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.
Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.
Two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of several London establishments that has opened in Dubai Photograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer “We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.
But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.
“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”
The British Michelin-starred chef Jason Atherton has previously spoken out about high taxes and the UK’s struggling hospitality sector. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Guardian Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.
Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”
