items.title: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
items.summary: As Nvidia has gone from chipmaker to industry financier, some investors see the company taking on outsized risk tied to the AI buildout.
items.content:
Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
As Nvidia has transitioned from chipmaker to industry financier, some investors see the company taking on outsized risk tied to the AI buildout.
Those concerns are showing up in the market with shares of neoclouds tanking and bond yields rising.
"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs.
Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.
Nvidia's emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners.
After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang's strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands.
That's meant taking full advantage of Nvidia's investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates.
As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties.
For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won't have to pay up unless participants in the project default.
"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview.
Market conditions may soon test Nvidia's mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN , all cash-burning companies in Nvidia's portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default.
Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges.
The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy . Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven't provided updates on their plans in weeks.
Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year.
Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."
"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital."
Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter.
Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers' hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process.
Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022.
Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia's flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate.
While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google , which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices , which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July.
AMD rivals Nvidia with first AI system, signing Microsoft and Meta
Cash is Nvidia's other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout.
That's a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.
Nvidia's most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class.
That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR's Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund.
"We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use," Huang told CNBC , in announcing the agreement in August. "But now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."
Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment.
"We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable," he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week.
While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space.
Nvidia's biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI's forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years.
The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.
If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia's guarantee ends.
At CoreWeave, Nvidia's investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can't find another taker.
Nvidia's backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia's deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.
"We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand," Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.
Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn't need Nvidia's backstop and that the neocloud's cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%.
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business.
CoreWeave and other neoclouds "will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?" Stutland said. "Is it going to break at some point?"
Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products.
"They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. "That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers."
Nvidia's credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing , published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements.
Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn't want to be in the position of insurer, "but they're willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up."
"They kind of control how things move," said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. "They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it."
Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs.
"Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem," said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. "But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions."
According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia's net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year.
Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody's have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said.
Moody's doesn't count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it's "something we're constantly monitoring," said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency.
"These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take," he said. Gonzales said it's likely that chips will retain "values in excess of contractual residual value amounts" in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia's financing structures.
Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is "the question we're evaluating at all times every day," Gonzales said.
"It's the center of all of our discussions right now," he said.
— CNBC's Seema Mody contributed to this report.

Here's the AI Chip Stock That Hedge Funds Are Loading Up On
We spend a fair bit of time covering and commenting on the investment moves made by leading hedge fund managers, such as Ken Griffin at Citadel, to inform investors about what some of the experts in the field are seeing.
Market intelligence firm Data Insights tracks the stocks that hedge funds buy and sell. Specifically, it produces a monthly crowding report that examines the most popular long and short positions held by hedge funds and institutional investors.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
September was a rocky month for large caps, as the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell, partly due to the Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates. But hedge fund managers saw this as a buying opportunity, particularly for large tech stocks .
Of the 10 stocks that hedge funds held the most in September, Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) was the most popular, followed by Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT). Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) were also in the top 10.
Image source: Getty Images. One of the biggest movers in the group was AI chipmaker Broadcom, which flipped from bearish in August, when it was mostly shorted, to bullish in September, when it was among the most-held long stocks.
Why are hedge funds back on board with Broadcom? Should you be, too?
Broadcom reported third-quarter earnings on Sept. 2 and posted impressive gains. Revenue jumped 86% year over year to $29.6 billion, beating estimates, while net income rose 216% to $13.1 billion or $2.68 per share. Its AI semiconductor revenue surged 221% year over year and 54% from the previous quarter to $16.7 billion. This also blew away estimates.
Some analysts didn't think the firm's forward guidance was good enough. But let's put this into perspective: Broadcom's revenue growth is expected to increase 93% year over year to $34.8 billion in Q4. Those gaudy projections were just short of analysts' estimates of $35.03 billion.
Further, the AI semiconductor revenue is expected to accelerate to $21.7 billion in Q4, up 236% year over year. Broadcom raised its AI semiconductor revenue guidance to $58 billion for fiscal 2026, up from $56 billion. That's up from $20 billion the previous year.
In 2027, the firm is targeting $115 billion in AI semiconductor revenue, up 98% from this year. And it expects to double that to $230 billion in 2028.
There have been other concerns about Broadcom, such as its declining gross margin, which is still attractive at 73%. But the decline stems from a rapidly growing mix of its lower-margin AI semiconductor business. However, that will eventually settle.
I think the major concern was its valuation, given its pretty incredible run over the past three years. Broadcom stock has averaged an annualized return of 59% over the past three years, with two years of triple-digit returns in 2023 and 2024.
It was bound to come back to earth a bit after its price-to-earnings ratio soared to over 100 a little over a year ago.
I think hedge funds saw the post-earnings dip and decided to pile back into Broadcom, given the company's strong growth and outlook for the next two years. Also, they likely saw the valuation as enticing, as Broadcom's P/E ratio is down to 46, but its forward P/E is just 19 and its five-year P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio is just 0.36.
Broadcom stock looks really attractive at these forward valuations, suggesting it may be undervalued relative to its long-term growth expectations. This should be a stock to put back on your radar.

European student protests take aim at Serbia’s elections Students have been protesting across Europe. In Serbia, they've selected candidates to run for parliament in Sunday's elections. And they're aiming to end 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vucic.
European student protests take aim at Serbia's elections
European student protests take aim at Serbia’s elections
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6012799/nx-s1-9977263" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Students have been protesting across Europe. In Serbia, they've selected candidates to run for parliament in Sunday's elections. And they're aiming to end 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vucic.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Students across Europe have been taking to the streets in protest. In Serbia, they're taking their movement to the ballot box, with a list of candidates ranging from academics and economists to athletes and engineers who are running in Sunday's parliamentary elections. They hope to end 14 years of rule by a populist leader in the Serbian Progressive Party. Guy De Launey reports from Serbia's capital, Belgrade. GUY DE LAUNEY, BYLINE: Tens of thousands of people are gathering here at Slavija Square in the center of Serbia's capital, Belgrade. They're turning out for the final pre-election rally of the Student List. That's the opposition movement, which emerged from the long-running student-led protests. Now it's posing the most serious challenge to Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vucic, since his Progressive Party took power in 2012. MIHAIL DUDAS: I want people to be free - to be free to say whatever they want, to be free to talk about the political situation, to talk about the solutions. LAUNEY: Mihail Dudas represented Serbia in the decathlon at two Olympic Games. Now he's among the people running for parliament on the Student List. DUDAS: I am very honored to be selected to be in 250 very, very smart, good, powerful people who are ready to basically change the direction in - for Serbia in the right direction. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) LAUNEY: Around 150,000 people attended the Student List rally this week, marking the culmination of a protest movement that started two years ago. That's when a concrete canopy collapsed at the recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city. Sixteen people died, and the disaster sparked student-led protests accusing Aleksandar Vucic of presiding over endemic corruption. He'd made infrastructure improvements a key part of his image as the strong leader steering Serbia into the future. So the station disaster has been hard for him to shake off. MAGDA ANASTASIJEVIC: The government expected the protests to die down after the initial spark. LAUNEY: Magda Anastasijevic is the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor ACLED. ANASTASIJEVIC: Vucic has survived this in the past. He was always find a - able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) LAUNEY: In the home of the student protest movement, the pre-election atmosphere seems calm. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) LAUNEY: The young people studying here in Novi Sad have been collaborating with colleagues around the country to choose the candidates for the Student List. They didn't put themselves forward. They deliberately selected candidates with no background in politics. VUK STOJIC: We are offering something new, something different. LAUNEY: Vuk Stojic is a law student at Novi Sad University. He's one of the activists who've been involved in selecting the candidates for the parliamentary elections. STOJIC: This is not only a student movement. It's a movement of all the free-thinking people in Serbia. And that's what gave us strength. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED RALLYGOERS: (Chanting in Serbian). LAUNEY: At pre-election rallies, Aleksandar Vucic has brushed off his critics' accusations of autocratic tendencies. He resigned as president last month because he couldn't serve a third term, and he's now hoping to stay in power as prime minister. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED RALLYGOERS: (Chanting in Serbian). LAUNEY: International monitors of previous elections have noted that Vucic's dominates the media and uses state resources for its own benefit. Many Serbians have been willing to overlook that as long as they accepted Vucic's carefully curated image as the protector of Serbia's interests. The Novi Sad disaster has undoubtedly damaged that, but Vucic remains defiant. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ALEXSANDAR VUCIC: (Speaking Serbian). LAUNEY: "We're going out there to win," he tells the crowd at this rally in Novi Sad. "We're going out there to defeat them, and we're going to deliver our biggest landslide victory yet." (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) LAUNEY: The Student List and the tens of thousands backing it beg to differ. For the first time in 14 years, Serbia's election looks uncertain. For NPR News, I'm Guy De Launey in Belgrade, Serbia.

items.content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters
More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff
Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro .
Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.
On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback . Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.
Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves to supporters on Saturday. Photograph: Dhavid Normando/AP “The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.
“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.
“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.
Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022 , as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.
However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.
People watch a televised debate between Flávio Bolsonaro and his election rival on Friday. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally – which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people – activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”
On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.
“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.
Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.
“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.
Lula supporters on Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.
Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.
Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.
Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George Monbiot
“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.
Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.
“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.
“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.
Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”
“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.
Some Lula supporters believe he can overturn the lead his rival secured in the first round of voting. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.
Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.
“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.
“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion , he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”
Bolsonaro supporters, some with the flags of the US, Israel and Brazil, also held last-minute rallies on Saturday. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”
Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.
Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.
“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

items.content:
Speaker Wetang'ula hails China's zero-tariff policy as boost to Kenyan farmers' income
Speaker of Kenya's National Assembly Moses Wetang'ula has hailed China's zero-tariff policy as a boost to Kenyan farmers' income.
Wetang'ula made the remarks in a recent interview with the China Media Group (CMG) in north China's Tianjin Municipality, where he attended the 2026 Legislators Forum for Friendly Exchanges.
Since May 1, China has expanded zero-tariff treatment to all African countries that have diplomatic relations with it. The inclusion of an additional 20 African nations under the policy demonstrates the nation's active commitment to expanding high-standard opening up, according to the authorities.
The policy means more Kenyan goods, including avocados, coffee and cut flowers, can enter the Chinese market with ease. Kenyan lawmakers, farmers and industry players say the benefits are already showing.
"That came as a boom for our economy. And we have seen our exports to China grow by leaps and bounds and now exporting more avocados. The farmers back home are happy we're now exporting more coffee. Our farmers are happy they are now getting more money. And I can tell you the demand has improved the income of farmers. Coffee farming is now booming," said Wetang'ula.
The zero-tariff arrangement has not only lifted Kenyan coffee and avocado exports but also reshaped how the country's world-leading cut-flower industry reaches buyers—shifting from a traditional route through Amsterdam to direct shipments to China, according to the speaker.
"Kenya is the leading country in the world in cut flowers. And traditionally all our flowers were headed to Amsterdam and then when they get there, they become the flowers of Holland. But now we are able to export our flowers to arrive in China as flowers and products of Kenya. And because of that, today we have daily flights from Nairobi to Guangzhou, the Kenyans and those flights are full. Duty-free, quota-free for us, open market for Chinese goods as well. So we have a booming trade going on between our two countries and I believe and we like it, we appreciate it and we see this as an act from a true friend to our country," said Wetang'ula.

French protesters grow increasingly disillusioned about future amid nationwide demonstrations
French protesters taking to the streets nationwide say they are growing increasingly frustrated and angry about the future as they struggle with the rising cost of living, deteriorating educational facilities and poor public services.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted in France on Oct 17, with the government estimating that approximately 550,000 people had participated across the country, while organizers claimed the figure reached 800,000.
In many cities, the protests escalated into violent unrest. In Paris, vehicles were set ablaze and shops were vandalized, while public facilities in several other cities also sustained varying degrees of damage.
The mass protests were initially triggered by students dissatisfied with a lack of educational resources and the poor condition of school facilities.
They were later joined by groups such as farmers and urban residents frustrated by rising energy prices, the high cost of living and declining public services.
Last week, protests in Marseille, France's second-largest city, descended into widespread violence.
On Oct 22, authorities in the Bouches-du-Rhone department, where Marseille is located, announced a ban on all protests across the department, including the southern port city, effective Oct 24.
High school students in Marseille say rising living costs and deteriorating school conditions are among the reasons they have taken to the streets.
"The price of gasoline and life itself have become too expensive. We have to protest, for the future, for ourselves and for our lives in the future," said Pablo Marez, a high school student.
"Overcrowding in classes, rats in classes. Walls in classes just don't stand up anymore. The heating doesn't work. During summer, it was way too hot," said Jenna, another high school student.
Observers said the protesters' demands highlight a series of governance challenges facing France, including a fiscal crisis, pressure on the welfare system and political polarization. With the 2027 presidential election approaching, some protesters say they see no candidate capable of turning the situation around.
"Currently, I don't see anyone who is capable of changing the situation in a country like France. I don't believe the answer lies in turning to the extremes or to the extremist parties -- whether it's the extreme right or the extreme left. People are becoming increasingly angry. We saw this on Saturday, October 17, and unfortunately, things are likely to get even worse in two days," said Jerome Borgeot, a social worker who works with homeless people in Marseille.

Marco Rubio in Mumbai, India, on 21 October. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/AP
Marco Rubio in Mumbai, India, on 21 October. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/AP
Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran
Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.
The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.
The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.
Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.
“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.
“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”
Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.
In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.
Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.
“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.
“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”
Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.
During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

items.title: Trump is pushing a massive AI buildout. His own voters are wary of what comes with it
items.summary: A new CNBC survey finds broad voter opposition to nearby AI data centers, creating a political challenge for Trump and Republicans ahead of the midterm election.
items.content:
Trump AI push faces voter backlash over data centers: CNBC survey
A new CNBC All-America Economic Survey finds 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
Republican voters broadly support continued AI development, but many oppose the data centers and power infrastructure needed to support it in their own communities.
The backlash is reshaping midterm election politics, pushing Republicans who once championed data-center investment to emphasize utility costs, local impacts and tougher safeguards.
Top 5 takeaways from CNBC's All America Economic Survey
President Donald Trump has cast America's artificial intelligence race with China as a national-security imperative, pushing faster development of the technology and an immense buildout of the data centers and power infrastructure needed to fuel it.
But the new CNBC All-America Economic Survey reveals a growing political tension beneath that agenda: Republican voters broadly support the push for AI development, but many oppose building the sprawling infrastructure needed to power it in their own backyards.
Nearly 55% of MAGA supporters want companies to keep developing advanced AI while Congress works on regulations, versus 27% who favor a pause. But only 29% would support a data center within 10 miles of their home, while 40% oppose one. Among all Republicans and Republican-leaning voters — not just those who identify themselves with the MAGA movement — those who say they would support a data center near their home falls to 24%.
Across the electorate, 63% don't want a nearby AI data center and just 13% support one. Democrats lead the opposition: 80% oppose nearby facilities while just 4% support them.
That resistance is increasingly forcing Trump and vulnerable Republicans who once championed data centers to recalibrate as they head into a bleak midterm election environment for the party.
"Many people are annoyed by these data centers," said Brad Carson , a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma and co-founder of Public First Action PAC, an AI-industry-backed political group pushing for stronger regulation and safeguards. "People are also strongly insistent upon reasonable guardrails of AI, and that's going to be hard to beat."
The CNBC survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide was conducted Oct. 14-18 by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The data-center proximity question was asked of a half-sample of roughly 500 voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.38 percentage points.
The politics have shifted from the early AI boom, when Washington and Silicon Valley sold the technology as an avenue for investment, growth and American dominance.
But as the buildout accelerates, its physical costs are becoming harder to ignore. Communities are fighting data centers over spiking electric bills , soaring electricity and water demand, noise, land use and taxpayer subsidies. Coupled with job- displacement fears from AI, opponents now point to the facilities as a physical symbol of who benefits from the boom and who gets stuck with the bill.
“The data center industry provides significant, tangible benefits,” said Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition, pointing to jobs, investment and tax revenue while adding that operators are committed to “paying for the energy we use."
But when asked their top concerns if Republicans retain Congress, 18% of voters in the survey cited a failure to regulate AI and data centers. That tied continued military efforts in Iran and outranked continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations at 15%, cuts to health insurance subsidies at 10% and an extension of Trump's tariffs at 5%.
Even among voters who want Republicans to retain control, 17% cited weak AI and data center oversight — second only to a failure to bring down prices.

America by the numbers: How voters feel about the economy, inflation and Trump
In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned AI companies that data center backlash was threatening Sen. Jon Husted's reelection in Ohio, calling the issue a midterm "sleeper" that could sour politicians nationwide on future projects, Axios reported .
As Ohio lieutenant governor in 2024, Husted helped announce a $10 billion Amazon Web Services expansion, calling AI facilities " crucial to America's economic superiority ." Now, in a tight Senate race against Democrat Sherrod Brown , who has made data-center opposition a campaign issue, Husted is promoting stalled legislation to make large facilities cover their own grid and generation costs rather than pass them on to residential ratepayers.
Texas tells a similar story. Less than a year after Gov. Greg Abbott hailed the state as an " epicenter of AI development ," he halted data center permits pending grid- and water-impact reviews and called for ending state tax incentives.
Trump himself is showing signs of the political pressure. In a Truth Social post Wednesday, he said data center developers should pay host communities a financial "dividend" and generate their own power, arguing that local payouts can turn unpopular projects into popular ones.
For now, Democrats hold a modest edge on managing the issue: 32% of voters trust them to handle data center expansion, versus 24% for the Republicans. But 27% said neither party would do a better job than the other.
And the CNBC survey indicates this skepticism runs deeper than local zoning. Overall, 52% of registered voters want advanced AI development paused until Congress passes safety regulations, compared to 32% who favor moving ahead to keep pace with China. Democrats remain far more cautious: 70% favor a pause, while just 18% support pushing forward.
"The debate has shifted dramatically," Carson told CNBC. "A year ago, there were many people who said, 'Let it cook, no regulation at all, exempt the companies from normal rules.'" Carson said sentiment toward AI has "deteriorated a lot over the last six months."

items.title: Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
items.summary: After almost 18 months, Berkshire Hathaway shares have entirely erased all the ground they lost in the wake of Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO.
items.content:
Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
After almost 18 months, Berkshire Hathaway shares have entirely erased all the ground they lost in the wake of Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
People watch as Berkshire Hathaway chairman Warren Buffett is seen on a screen speaking at the Berkshire Hathaway annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on May 3, 2025.
On Friday, May 2, 2025, the  Class A shares closed at $809,350. The Class B shares finished at $539.80.
The meeting was the following day, Saturday, May 3.
On Monday, May 5, BRK.A dropped 4.9% and BRK.B lost 5.1%.
CNBC.com noted a 14% drop in Q1 operating earnings , also announced that Saturday, may have contributed to the declines.
It also relayed some reassurance from analysts like Brian Meredith at UBS who predicted the company's culture and strategy would "remain unchanged" under new CEO Greg Abel.
"Buffett leaves a company that is less reliant on his investing capabilities, with an array of leading businesses with strong cash flows."
As the stock fell, there were fears a " Buffett premium " was evaporating.
Three months later, at their lowest closes of the year, BRK.A had lost 14.3% of its value and the more widely held B shares were down almost 15%.
Since then, they've rallied by 18%, and on Tuesday this week both classes topped their pre-announcement levels to set fresh all-time closing highs.
They were higher still on Thursday, setting new closing highs of $820,500 and $546.97.
Friday they lost almost 1% but remain roughly one-half of a percentage point above their highs just before the 2025 meeting.
Berkshire's gains have reduced its year-to-date deficit against the benchmark S&P to less than four percentage points.
A majority of the net gain in points between the August 2025 low and now has been racked up this month.
Berkshire's B shares have gained almost 9% since the start of October, strongly outperforming the S&P 500's dip of 0.4% and an almost 4.8% drop for the equal-weight NYSE Fang+ index , which tracks 10 megacap tech names , including Meta , NVIDIA , and Alphabet .
Investors have been rotating out of high-flying tech and AI stocks in recent weeks amid growing concerns their massive spending on computing infrastructure won't produce the sustained profits they envision .
Berkshire, by contrast, is "the ultimate anti-AI play," according to a Barron's headline this week.
"With more than $350 billion in cash and equivalents on its balance sheet and close to $50 billion of annual after-tax earnings from a diverse group of businesses, Berkshire arguably is the most defensive megacap stock in the market."
And on CNBC's "Morning Call" Monday morning , Adam Patti of VistaShares, which runs an ETF that tracks Berkshire's portfolio , said the market's turn away from its long-running "momentum-driven frenzy" comes at a good time.
"The market spent a year pricing Berkshire without Buffett. I think it's finally decided Abel can, in fact, run it" and likes that he's taking advantage of the company's cash.
"Berkshire is a coiled spring. When it comes back, it comes back fast and furious."
Top Berkshire watcher on why the market has finally realized Greg Abel can run the company
But, as Patti notes, Berkshire isn't completely separated from the AI world.
CEO Greg Abel has said providing energy to the growing number of AI data centers is a " significant opportunity for Berkshire and Berkshire Hathaway Energy " as long as rates don't rise for its other customers.
And Berkshire has a now $34 billion position in Alphabet , one of AI's biggest players.

Berkshire's hidden multi-billion-dollar mistakes (2001)
Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett admit their biggest errors are often "mistakes of omission" that don't appear in Berkshire's balance sheet.
Berkshire's hidden multi-billion-dollar mistakes
AUDIENCE MEMBER : Mr. Munger, I know you're fond of evoking humility to promote rational thought. So my question is, what's the most recent business mistake that you've made, Mr. Munger, and why did it occur? (Laughter)
WARREN BUFFETT : I'm going to take notes on this one. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER : The mistakes that have been most extreme in Berkshire's history are mistakes of omission. They don't show up in our figures. They show up in opportunity costs.
In other words, we have opportunities, we almost do it. In retrospect, we can tell that we were very much mistaken not to do it.
In terms of the shareholders, those are the ones in our history that it really cost the most. And very few managements do much thinking or talking about opportunity costs.
WARREN BUFFETT : Billions and billions and billions. I might as well say it. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER : Right, right. And we keep doing it. (Laughter)
WARREN BUFFETT : Some might say we're getting better at it. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER : I don't like mentioning the specific companies, because the — you know, we may, in due course, want to buy them again and have an opportunity to do so at our price.
But practically everywhere in life, and in corporate life, too, what really costs, in comparison with what easily might have been, are the blown opportunities. I mean, it just — it's an awesome amount of money...
WARREN BUFFETT : I might add that when we speak of errors of omission, of which we've had plenty, and some very big ones, we don't mean not buying some stock where we — a friend runs it, or we know the name and it went from one to 100. That doesn't mean anything. It's only —
We only regard errors as being things that are within our circle of competence.
So if somebody knows how to make money in cocoa beans, or they know how to make money in a software company or anything, and we miss that, that is not an error, as far as we're concerned.
What's an error is when it's something we understand, and we stand there and stare at it, and we don't do anything.
Or worse yet, what really gets me is when we do something very small with it. We do an eyedropper's worth of it, when we could do it very big.
Charlie refers to that elegantly when I do that sort of thing as when I'm sucking my thumb. (Laughter)
And there really — I mean, we have been thumbsuckers at times with businesses that we understood well.
And it may have been because we started buying, and the price moved up a little, and we waited around hoping we would get more at the price we originally started — there could be a lot of things.
But those are huge mistakes. Conventional accounting, of course, does not pick those up at all. But they're in our scorebook.
